Between 1985 and 1988, Karikó was a postdoctoral fellow at [Temple University](/wiki/Temple_University "Temple University") in Philadelphia. Karikó participated in a clinical trial in which patients with AIDS, [hematologic diseases](/wiki/Hematologic_disease "Hematologic disease"), and [chronic fatigue syndrome](/wiki/Chronic_fatigue_syndrome "Chronic fatigue syndrome") were treated with [double-stranded RNA](/wiki/RNA#Double-stranded_RNA "RNA") (dsRNA). At the time, this was considered groundbreaking research, as the molecular mechanism of [interferon](/wiki/Interferon "Interferon") induction by dsRNA was not known, although the antiviral and [antineoplastic](/wiki/Antineoplastic "Antineoplastic") effects of interferons were well-documented.[[39]](#cite_note-39)

In 1988, Karikó accepted a job at [Johns Hopkins University](/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_University "Johns Hopkins University") without first informing her lab advisor Suhadolnik of her intention to leave Temple, as recounted in [Gregory Zuckerman](/wiki/Gregory_Zuckerman "Gregory Zuckerman")'s 2021 book *A Shot to Save the World*. Suhadolnik told her that if she went to Johns Hopkins, he would have her [deported](/wiki/Deportation "Deportation"), and subsequently reported her to U.S. immigration authorities, claiming that she was "illegally" in the United States. In the time it took her to successfully challenge the resulting extradition order, Johns Hopkins withdrew the job offer. Suhadolnik "continued bad-mouthing Karikó, making it impossible for her to get a new position" at other institutions, until she met a researcher at [Bethesda Naval Hospital](/wiki/Bethesda_Naval_Hospital "Bethesda Naval Hospital") who "had his own difficult history with Suhadolnik".[[40]](#cite_note-Zuckerman2021-40) Karikó subsequently confirmed that the incident had happened as Zuckerman described, but emphasized that "more importantly I was always grateful to [Suhadolnik for] sending me the [IAP66 form](/wiki/U.S._Immigration_and_Customs_Enforcement "U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement") in 1985, for the opportunity he gave me to work in his lab", noting that "when I gave a

fanoutqa_003583.t: Mount Everest :: Flora and fauna :: chunk_0014
fanoutqa_003583.x:
Mount Everest :: Flora and fauna :: chunk_0014
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Yak_at_third_lake_in_Gokyo.jpg/250px-Yak_at_third_lake_in_Gokyo.jpg)](/wiki/File:Yak_at_third_lake_in_Gokyo.jpg)

A yak at around 4,790 m (15,720 ft)

There is very little native flora or fauna on Everest. A type of [moss](/wiki/Moss "Moss") grows at 6,480 metres (21,260 ft) on Mount Everest and it may be the highest altitude plant species.[[68]](#cite_note-75) An alpine cushion plant called *[Arenaria](/wiki/Arenaria_(plant) "Arenaria (plant)")* is known to grow below 5,500 metres (18,000 ft) in the region.[[69]](#cite_note-autumn-76) According to the study based on satellite data from 1993 to 2018, vegetation is expanding in the Everest region. Researchers have found plants in areas that were previously deemed bare.[[70]](#cite_note-77)

A minute black [jumping spider](/wiki/Jumping_spider "Jumping spider") of the genus *[Euophrys](/wiki/Euophrys "Euophrys")* has been found at elevations as high as 6,700 metres (22,000 ft),[[71]](#cite_note-wanless-78) possibly making it the highest confirmed non-microscopic permanent resident on Earth. Another Euophrys species, *E. everestensis*, has been found at 5,030 metres (16,500 ft), and may feed on insects that have been blown there by the wind.[[71]](#cite_note-wanless-78) There is a high likelihood of microscopic life at even higher altitudes.

The [bar-headed goose](/wiki/Bar-headed_goose "Bar-headed goose") migrates over the Himalayas and have been seen flying at the higher altitudes of the mountain.[[72]](#cite_note-his7-79) In 1953, George Lowe (part of the expedition of Tenzing and Hillary) said that he saw bar-headed geese flying over Everest's summit.[[73]](#cite_note-80) Another bird species, the [chough](/wiki/Chough "Chough"), have been spotted as high as the [South Col](/wiki/South_Col "South Col") at 7,906 m (25,938 ft)[[74]](#cite_note-81) and [yellow-billed choughs](/wiki/Yellow-billed_chough "Yellow-billed chough") have been seen as high as 7,900 m (25,919 ft).[[72]](#cite_note-his7-79)

HP Inc. :: History :: As Hewlett-Packard :: chunk_0001
Main article: [Hewlett-Packard § History](/wiki/Hewlett-Packard#History "Hewlett-Packard")

Hewlett-Packard was founded in 1939 by [Bill Hewlett](/wiki/Bill_Hewlett "Bill Hewlett") and [David Packard](/wiki/David_Packard "David Packard"), who both graduated with degrees in [electrical engineering](/wiki/Electrical_engineering "Electrical engineering") from [Stanford University](/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University") in 1935. The company started off in the [HP Garage](/wiki/HP_Garage "HP Garage") in [Palo Alto, California](/wiki/Palo_Alto,_California "Palo Alto, California").

In March 2015, HP announced that [Bang & Olufsen](/wiki/Bang_%26_Olufsen "Bang & Olufsen") would become the company's new premium audio partner for its computers and other devices. This replaced the partnership with [Beats Electronics](/wiki/Beats_Electronics "Beats Electronics") that ended upon being acquired by [Apple Inc.](/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.") in 2014.[[6]](#cite_note-cnet-bando-6)

On November 1, 2015, Hewlett-Packard was split into two companies. Its personal computer and printer businesses became HP Inc., while its enterprise business became [Hewlett Packard Enterprise](/wiki/Hewlett_Packard_Enterprise "Hewlett Packard Enterprise"). The split was structured so that Hewlett-Packard changed its name to HP Inc. and spun off Hewlett Packard Enterprise as a new publicly traded company. HP Inc. retains Hewlett-Packard's pre-2015 stock price history and its former stock ticker symbol, HPQ, while Hewlett Packard Enterprise trades under its own symbol, HPE.[[3]](#cite_note-Chan-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Darrow-4)[[7]](#cite_note-7)

**Brentford Football Club** is a professional [association football](/wiki/Association_football "Association football") club based in [London](/wiki/London "London"), England. The team competes in the [Premier League](/wiki/Premier_League "Premier League"), the top tier of [English football](/wiki/English_football_league_system "English football league system"). Nicknamed "The Bees", the club was founded in 1889 and played home matches at [Griffin Park](/wiki/Griffin_Park "Griffin Park") from 1904 before moving to the [Brentford Community Stadium](/wiki/Brentford_Community_Stadium "Brentford Community Stadium") in 2020.

Brentford initially played amateur football before they entered the [London League](/wiki/London_League_(football) "London League (football)") in 1896 and finished as runners-up of the Second Division and then the First Division to win election into the [Southern League](/wiki/Southern_Football_League "Southern Football League") in 1898. As of September 30, 2020, Alphabet Inc. had 132,121 employees,[[271]](#cite_note-272) of which more than 100,000 worked for Google.[[8]](#cite_note-Wakabayashi2019-9) Google's 2020 diversity report states that 32 percent of its workforce are women and 68 percent are men, with the ethnicity of its workforce being predominantly white (51.7%) and Asian (41.9%).[[272]](#cite_note-273) Within tech roles, 23.6 percent were women; and 26.7 percent of leadership roles were held by women.[[273]](#cite_note-274) In addition to its 100,000+ full-time employees, Google used about 121,000 temporary workers and contractors, as of March 2019.[[8]](#cite_note-Wakabayashi2019-9)

The British Shorthair publicity from 19th and 20th century cat shows helped British Shorthairs become one of the most popular pet cat breeds today. For example, in the 1980s, the British Shorthair was featured in competition by the CFA, which led to an increased demand for British Shorthairs as household pets. As of 2023, the British Shorthair ranks as the 6th most popular cat breed in the United States.[[10]](#cite_note-10) According to the GCCF's 2024 registry data, it is once again the most popular pedigreed breed in its native country, accounting for about half of the annually registered kittens.[[1]](#cite_note-GCCFprof-1)[[11]](#cite_note-11) And it has held the title of the UK's most popular cat breed for decades.[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13) In the 2024 statistics of [FIFe](/wiki/F%C3%A9d%C3%A9ration_Internationale_F%C3%A9line "Fédération Internationale Féline"), one of the major global [cat registries](/wiki/Cat_registries "Cat registries"), the breed ranked at position 2 out of 54 breeds in popularity, comprising 16.9% of their total registered kittens that year, which translates to 16.278 cats.[[14]](#cite_note-FIFestat-14)

**Mars** is the fourth [planet](/wiki/Planet "Planet") from the [Sun](/wiki/Sun "Sun"). It is also known as the "**Red Planet**", for [its orange-red](/wiki/Mars_surface_color "Mars surface color") appearance.[[22]](#cite_note-Rees2012-24)[[23]](#cite_note-nasa_hematite-25) Mars is a desert-like [rocky planet](/wiki/Rocky_planet "Rocky planet") with a tenuous [atmosphere](/wiki/Atmosphere_of_Mars "Atmosphere of Mars") that is primarily [carbon dioxide](/wiki/Carbon_dioxide "Carbon dioxide") (CO2). At the average surface level the atmospheric pressure is a few thousandths of [Earth](/wiki/Earth "Earth")'s, atmospheric temperature ranges from −153 to 20 °C (−243 to 68 °F),[[24]](#cite_note-p167-26) and [cosmic radiation](/wiki/Cosmic_radiation "Cosmic radiation") is high. Mars retains some water, [in the ground](/wiki/Groundwater_on_Mars "Groundwater on Mars") as well as thinly in the atmosphere, forming [cirrus clouds](/wiki/Cirrus_cloud "Cirrus cloud"), [fog](/wiki/Fog "Fog"), [frost](/wiki/Frost "Frost"), larger polar regions of [permafrost](/wiki/Permafrost "Permafrost") and [ice caps](/wiki/Martian_polar_ice_caps "Martian polar ice caps") (with seasonal CO2 snow), but no bodies of liquid surface water. Its surface gravity is roughly a third of Earth's or double that of the Moon. Its diameter, 6,779 km (4,212 mi), is about [half the Earth](/wiki/List_of_Solar_System_objects_by_size "List of Solar System objects by size")'s, or twice the Moon's, and its surface area is the size of all the dry land of Earth.[[25]](#cite_note-27)

[Fine dust](/wiki/Martian_regolith#Atmospheric_dust "Martian regolith") is prevalent across the surface and the atmosphere, being picked up and spread at the low Martian gravity even by the weak wind of the tenuous atmosphere.
The terrain of Mars roughly follows a north–south divide, the [Martian dichotomy](/wiki/Martian_dichotomy "Martian dichotomy"), with the northern hemisphere mainly consisting of relatively flat, low lying [plains](/wiki/Plain "Plain"), and the southern hemisphere of cratered [highlands](/wiki/Highland "Highland"). Opening day took place in the Czech Republic, Voracek's birthplace. The Flyers beat the Blackhawks 4–2. The Flyers started off the season very well, tying a team record for the best November in team history with a record of 10–3–4.[[50]](#cite_note-53) The Flyers produced consistent, cohesive hockey throughout the season. One of the most notable progressions in the team was the chemistry of the team and the success of the second line, which consisted of [Scott Laughton](/wiki/Scott_Laughton "Scott Laughton"), Kevin Hayes, and [Travis Konecny](/wiki/Travis_Konecny "Travis Konecny"). In February, the team pulled away from the pack of Wild-Card spot chasers and reached second place in the Metropolitan Division following a home win against the Rangers that put their February record at 9–3. The Flyers ended up with a nine-game winning streak, losing at home against the Boston Bruins, the NHL's points leader. The Flyers were scheduled to play at Tampa Bay on March 12, but the NHL suspended all games earlier in the day due to [COVID-19 concerns](/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_North_America "COVID-19 pandemic in North America"). The Flyers were second in the Metropolitan Division, only 1 point behind the Capitals.
